what_it_does: Modern chips sometimes combine processors that speak different instruction sets (ISAs — the language a chip understands, such as x86 used in most laptops or RISC-V used in many embedded chips) on the same piece of silicon. Today, each ISA runs its own separate operating system (OS) kernel — the core software that manages hardware — which must communicate with the other kernels via message passing, adding overhead and preventing features like shared memory addresses across the two processor types. Stramash introduces a fused-kernel OS: a single Linux kernel that runs on all processor types simultaneously, using the fact that all cores share the same physical memory to read and write the same OS data structures directly without messaging. A prototype called Stramash-Linux and an accompanying multi-ISA simulator, Stramash-QEMU, are built to validate the approach.
